short: Pipe welded in a fixed 45° axis — the hardest standard position, and the one that proves a pipe welder.
long: The pipe cannot be turned, so the welder works uphill, overhead and vertically in one run. A 6G qualification usually covers all the easier positions beneath it. 6GR adds a restriction ring, which mimics welding next to an obstruction.

short: Pipe fixed horizontally, welder moves around it — vertical and overhead, but no 45° tilt.
Pipe or plate welded horizontally with the axis vertical. Easier than 5G and 6G.
Flat position (ISO). The easiest — the weld pool sits in the joint.
Horizontal-vertical (ISO): welding along a horizontal line on a vertical surface.
Overhead (ISO). Gravity works against the weld pool throughout.
Vertical up (ISO). Slow and controlled; the position most often asked for on structural work.
Vertical down (ISO). Faster than PF and used on thinner material; not interchangeable with it.
The welder qualification standard. Valid only for the process, position, material and thickness range printed on the certificate.
long: A certificate is not a general licence. Read the range: a welder qualified 6G on 8 mm carbon steel with 141 is not qualified for 20 mm duplex with 111. Validity usually needs a six-monthly employer endorsement.

short: MMA / stick welding (ISO process number). Slow, portable, forgiving of wind — common offshore and on repairs.
MAG welding with solid wire. Fast, used in shops and yards, poor in wind.
MAG welding with flux-cored wire. Higher deposition; common on heavy structural work.
TIG welding. Clean and precise, used for root runs on pipe and for stainless and duplex.
Welding Procedure Specification — the written recipe a welder must follow: process, consumable, heat, positions.
The test record proving a WPS produces a sound weld. The procedure's evidence, not the welder's.
A preliminary WPS, not yet qualified by a test.
A stainless steel with roughly equal austenite and ferrite. Strong and corrosion-resistant, unforgiving of heat input — welders are qualified for it separately.
A higher-alloy duplex used subsea. Narrow heat-input window; a scarce qualification.
Near-white blast cleaning to ISO 8501-1 — the surface standard most offshore coating specs demand.
long: Judged visually against photographic standards: no more than light shadows or staining on 5% of any area. Sa 3 is white metal, Sa 2 is thorough but leaves more residue.

short: White metal blast — the highest cleanliness grade in ISO 8501-1.
The standard defining blast-cleaning grades by photographic comparison.
Dry Film Thickness — coating thickness once cured, in microns. What the inspector actually measures.
Wet Film Thickness — measured with a comb during application to predict the DFT.
The Norwegian surface-treatment standard. Its coating systems are named by number and referenced across the North Sea.
Norwegian surface-treatment inspector scheme. Levels I–III; level II or III is what most yards ask for.
The body formed from NACE and SSPC. Its coating-inspector certification sits alongside FROSIO.
The former corrosion-engineering body, now part of AMPP. Old certificates still say NACE.
A high-voltage spark test for pinholes in a coating. A 'holiday' is a gap in the film.
Non-Destructive Testing — checking welds and materials without cutting them.
Ultrasonic Testing — sound through the material to find internal flaws.
Phased Array UT — a steered beam giving a cross-sectional image. Often replaces radiography offshore.
Time of Flight Diffraction — a UT technique that sizes flaws accurately. Usually paired with PAUT.
Magnetic Particle Testing — surface and near-surface cracks in ferrous material.
Penetrant Testing — dye drawn into surface-breaking cracks. Works on non-magnetic material.
Radiographic Testing — X-ray or gamma through the weld. Needs exclusion zones, so it is often night work.
Visual Testing — the first and cheapest inspection, and a formal qualification in its own right.
The UK personnel certification scheme for NDT, run by BINDT. Levels 1, 2 and 3 per method.
The international standard for qualifying NDT personnel. PCN is one scheme that certifies to it.
TWI's certification scheme. 3.1 is the standard welding inspector grade; 3.2 is senior.
An NDT technician who performs and reports inspections to a written procedure. Level 3 writes the procedures.
Basic Offshore Safety Induction and Emergency Training — the offshore entry ticket, including helicopter escape.
long: Usually valid four years, refreshed by FOET. OPITO and Norwegian GOF versions are not always interchangeable; check which the client accepts.

short: Further Offshore Emergency Training — the BOSIET refresher.
Helicopter Underwater Escape Training, the module inside BOSIET that people mean when they say 'the dunker'.
The UK-based offshore training standards body. OPITO BOSIET is the common UK/international ticket.
The Norwegian offshore safety course. Norway often requires it rather than OPITO BOSIET.
Global Wind Organisation training — the safety baseline for wind sites, recorded in WINDA.
Basic Safety Training: first aid, manual handling, fire awareness, working at heights, and sea survival offshore.
GWO's training record database. A WINDA ID is how a wind client checks the training is real.
Dutch/Belgian safety certification (SCC). VCA Basis for workers, VCA VOL for supervisors — asked for on most Benelux sites.
Safety Certificate Contractors — the international name for VCA.
The Norwegian offshore medical certificate. Without it nobody boards.
The fitness examination required before offshore work. OGUK in the UK, Helseattest in Norway.
The UK offshore medical, now issued under Offshore Energies UK. Usually two years.
The UK scaffolder card scheme. Part 1, Part 2, Advanced and Supervisor grades.
Rope access certification, levels 1–3. A level 3 must be on site to supervise and run the rescue plan.
The North American rope-access scheme. Broadly parallel to IRATA; not always accepted in Europe.
Work inside tanks, voids and ballast compartments. Needs its own training, a permit, and a standby man.
The written authorisation for hot work, confined space or work at height. No permit, no job.
Safe Job Analysis — the pre-task risk talk. Norwegian sites run these constantly and in English offshore.
The short briefing before a task. A candidate's English is judged on whether they can follow one.
The EU certificate showing which country's social security a posted worker pays into. Without it a client can be fined.
long: Issued by the home country's authority for a named posting and period. It is not a work permit and does not replace right to work.

short: Someone employed in one EU country and sent to work temporarily in another. Carries A1 and local pay rules.
Whether a person may legally work in the country the job is in. An EU passport covers the EU/EEA and does NOT cover the UK.
UK immigration status for EU nationals resident before 2021. Pre-settled is the five-year version.
Two weeks on site, two weeks off. The commonest offshore rotation.
Four weeks on, two off. Common on longer-haul and yard work.
The on/off pattern of a posting, written as days or weeks on to off.
Everything between accepting a job and standing on site: documents, medical, travel, induction.
Demobilisation — the end of a posting and the journey home.
The client pays the worker's rate and RFBT's margin separately, both visible.
One rate covering pay, margin and usually travel and accommodation. Simpler for the client, riskier for the agency.
What the client is billed per hour or day, as opposed to what the worker is paid.
What the worker receives, before allowances.
Engineering, Procurement and Construction — a contractor who takes a whole scope and hires the trades for it.
EPC plus Installation — the offshore version, including offshore construction.
The owner or operator of the asset. Above the EPC contractor in the chain.
Transport and Installation — the offshore campaign that puts foundations, turbines or structures in place.
Operations and Maintenance — the years of work after construction. Steady demand rather than a spike.
Maintenance, Modification and Operation — the Norwegian term for a long-running offshore maintenance frame agreement.
A planned stop to do work that cannot be done while running. Short, intense, and heavy on trades.
The refinery and process-plant word for a shutdown.
Final Investment Decision — the point a project is committed and hiring becomes real.
A multi-year contract to supply work or people as called off. Winning one is years of demand.
An individual order placed under a frame agreement.
The single steel tube driven into the seabed to carry an offshore turbine. Heavy welding, blasting and coating.
The section joining a monopile to the tower. Fabrication-heavy: welding, coating, bolting, platforms.
A steel lattice foundation for deeper water. Very heavy welding and NDT scope.
Everything above the water on an offshore platform. Piping, structures, electrical, insulation.
